Case study 02 · Okonkwo FinTech Solutions

From reactive support
to proactive success.

Designing a scalable Customer Success approach that uses product-usage signals to identify where customers may need help—and human judgement to understand why.

Project context

The scenario

This project explores how Okonkwo FinTech Solutions could support SME customers more proactively. In the case, Ihuoma Fashion House stopped using its inventory-reconciliation feature for five weeks. A check-in revealed that a new store manager had not been trained, so the team had returned to error-prone spreadsheets.

The customer problem

The customer’s reduced feature usage was an early sign that something had changed. The underlying issue was not simply a software defect: a new team member lacked training, and the customer had reverted to a manual workaround. Separately, a support agent resolved an invoicing bug in one day—an example of reactive support addressing a reported issue.

The scenario concludes with the CEO renewing and upgrading after the team retrained the store manager, shared a guide, scheduled a follow-up and introduced a bulk-upload feature the CEO had not known about.

The wider business challenge

The presentation identifies three scaling questions: how to decide which of thousands of SME accounts should receive proactive attention; how to use product-usage data consistently across the customer base; and how to balance high-touch service with the cost of serving many customers.

My proposed approach

Build an early-warning and action workflow

I propose using meaningful product-usage changes as prompts for investigation—not as automatic proof that an account is at risk. A scalable workflow can detect changes, prioritise accounts for review and support the Customer Success team in taking the right next step.

How the process works

  1. Monitor meaningful activity: define the product actions that indicate customer value and track changes over time.
  2. Detect and prioritise: identify unusual drops or abandoned feature usage so the team can focus attention.
  3. Investigate with the customer: book a check-in, ask what has changed and diagnose the root cause.
  4. Take a relevant action: provide retraining, share guidance, introduce useful features or coordinate a technical fix.
  5. Follow up: check whether adoption improves and whether the customer is realising value.

Customer Success vs. Customer Support

Customer Success is proactive: it looks for changes in behaviour, reaches out before a problem is reported, diagnoses root causes, supports adoption and builds long-term relationships.

Customer Support is reactive: it responds to reported issues, resolves tickets against service-level expectations, prioritises incidents and escalates or closes cases.

Both functions matter. Support resolves immediate problems; Customer Success works to help customers achieve outcomes and continue receiving value.

Risks and safeguards

Usage data can mislead if meaningful activity is poorly defined or measured. Low usage may reflect seasonality, business changes, feature relevance or technical issues—not necessarily customer dissatisfaction.

To reduce false-positive alerts, I recommend a human-in-the-loop process: the system detects and prioritises a signal, a CSM investigates, the root cause is identified, and an appropriate action is taken. Product data should be combined with direct customer conversations and feedback.

Guiding principle

Automation finds where attention is needed. Customer Success understands why and decides what to do.

This is the shift from reactive support to proactive Customer Success.

What this project demonstrates

Customer-health thinking · Product-adoption monitoring · Proactive outreach · Root-cause discovery · Customer education · Churn-risk awareness · Human-centred automation · Cross-functional problem solving.

Project note: This is a strategy/design case study based on the supplied presentation and its illustrative customer scenario. The deck does not provide verified portfolio-wide retention results or measured implementation outcomes, so none are claimed here.

Case study 01 · GreenCart business operations project

One connected journey.
A better customer experience.

Designing an integrated operations solution for a growing Lagos e-commerce business using HubSpot, Zendesk, ClickUp, Google Drive and Zapier.

Project context

The business

GreenCart is a growing e-commerce business based in Lagos, selling organic food, natural skincare and eco-friendly household products. The project brief describes a business serving more than 1,200 active weekly customers, with orders arriving through Instagram, WhatsApp and a basic website.

The challenge

Customer complaints were spread across Instagram, WhatsApp and email without central tracking. There was no CRM to manage customer, order and payment information; marketing attribution was unclear; delivery confirmation relied on manual WhatsApp messages; and there was no structured follow-up after complaints were resolved.

My proposed solution

I designed an integrated business operations system to connect customer-facing channels with sales, support and internal operations:

  • HubSpot CRM: central customer database, deal pipeline, customer segmentation and post-purchase communication.
  • Zendesk: central ticketing for customer complaints and enquiries from multiple channels, including auto-responses and macro responses.
  • ClickUp: internal task ownership for order processing, inventory checks, delivery coordination and marketing workflows.
  • Google Drive: shared repository for product catalogues, receipts, supplier invoices and operational records, supported by a live order/payment/delivery tracker.
  • Zapier: automation connecting systems for refund requests and delivery confirmation updates.

End-to-end customer journey

  1. Awareness and contact: customer reaches out via Instagram, WhatsApp or website; contact information is captured in HubSpot.
  2. Order creation and processing: the order is managed through the HubSpot deals pipeline, with order and payment progress updated.
  3. Complaint submission: customer issues become Zendesk tickets for tracking.
  4. Issue resolution: internal work is assigned and monitored in ClickUp.
  5. Delivery confirmation: delivery status is recorded in HubSpot and Google Sheets.
  6. Post-purchase follow-up: segmented automated emails support engagement and repeat purchases.

Automation workflows

The project outlines two automation use cases: a refund-request workflow connecting ClickUp and HubSpot, and a delivery-confirmation workflow connecting HubSpot, Zendesk and Google Sheets. These are designed to reduce manual updates and keep operational records aligned.

Intended business value

The proposed system is designed to centralise customer information, improve visibility across sales, support and delivery, reduce manual handling of complaints and delivery updates, and create more consistent post-purchase communication to support customer retention.

Customer Success capabilities demonstrated

Customer journey mapping, CRM design, support workflow design, customer communication, cross-functional process coordination, retention-oriented follow-up, operational automation and tool integration.

Project note: This is presented as a designed business operations solution. The source presentation describes the proposed system and its intended value; it does not provide measured before-and-after performance results.

Case study 07 · Sunrise Digital MFB

One experience.
Three connected moments.

A board-ready Customer Experience review connecting onboarding, Voice of the Customer, the full customer journey and service recovery.

The case

Where customers were being lost

Sunrise Digital MFB is presented as a fast-growing microfinance bank headquartered in Ikeja, Lagos, with agents across Ogun, Oyo and Kwara. Its digital account-opening push through Sunrise Pocket was designed to reach younger customers and reduce banking-hall queues. The review was framed as one joined-up customer experience story rather than separate fixes for onboarding, feedback and journey design.

The evidence

The case data shows a 12.02% overall 30-day activation yield. The largest headcount loss occurs at BVN/NIN verification, with 11,350 customers lost there, while the largest rate-based drop is between terms acceptance and first deposit at 52.99%. The review also highlights failed transfers, repeated logouts and fragmented feedback across four channels.

Root-cause thinking

The customer scenarios show different reasons behind the numbers: a lost verification session with no recovery path; unfamiliar account-tier names; no confirmation that documents were received; and no contact after registration. The recommendation is therefore not to treat every drop-off as the same problem, but to design recovery, clarity and confirmation into the journey.

Voice of the Customer operating model

I structured the proposed VoC process as: Capture → Classify → Consolidate & Theme → Prioritise → Assign & Act → Measure & Close the Loop. The prototype includes a feedback inbox, a theme/priority dashboard and an action tracker so issues can move from scattered comments to owned actions.

Moments of truth

Three priority moments are addressed: onboarding with save-and-resume verification and clearer progress; first use with transaction status, reference numbers and resolution times; and ongoing-use recovery with acknowledgement, ownership and real follow-up. The intended emotional shift is from frustration or anxiety toward confidence and reassurance.

Roadmap & ownership

The proposed sequence is to stabilise transactions first, redesign onboarding in parallel, embed the Voice of the Customer process, and then review and improve continuously. Ownership is assigned across Operations, Customer Experience and all relevant owners.

What this demonstrates

Customer journey mapping, onboarding analysis, Voice of the Customer design, root-cause analysis, service recovery, cross-functional ownership, prioritisation and translating customer evidence into an actionable CX roadmap.

Project note: This is presented as a review/strategy project based on the supplied case. The source contains case data and recommendations, not verified implementation results, so the portfolio does not present the proposed fixes as completed outcomes.

Case study 08 · Akwete Pay

Recover trust.
Restore activity.
Grow sustainably.

A merchant retention and recovery operating plan built around verified root causes, service recovery, reactivation and responsible account growth.

The business problem

A serious retention signal

Akwete Pay is presented as a Lagos-based fintech providing POS terminals and card-payment processing to merchants. The case uses an Onitsha market cluster of 2,400 merchants. Monthly cluster volume fell from ₦6.2bn in October 2025 to ₦4.9bn in January 2026, a 21% decline, while failed transactions rose from 2% in October to 7% in December. The case also identifies 312 merchants inactive for 30 days.

What merchants said

Interviews with 40 of the 312 inactive merchants surfaced late settlement as the leading reported issue (18 interviewees / 45%), followed by slow reversals (11 / 27.5%), competition (7 / 17.5%) and other reasons such as faulty terminals or closed shops (4 / 10%). The plan explicitly treats these interviews as directional evidence and calls for individual diagnosis of the full cohort.

Priority account: Ifeoma Superstores

The case focuses on a high-value merchant whose monthly volume fell from ₦48m in October 2025 to ₦17m in January 2026, a 64.6% decline, while the terminal remained active. Three pending reversals totalled ₦410,000. The first actions are to acknowledge the disruption, trace the transactions, assign one accountable owner, provide realistic updates, confirm the first successful transaction, then follow up at day 7 and day 30.

Two workstreams, not outreach alone

Workstream A — Operational fixes: confirm settlement and reversal standards, investigate transaction failures, strengthen monitoring and outage communication, and clear tickets older than five days. Workstream B — Merchant recovery: contact the cohort, diagnose causes, resolve cases, support successful transactions and monitor sustained activity.

The 90-day recovery playbook

Day 1–7: contact outcomes, root causes and owners for all 312 accounts. Day 8–30: establish baselines, target at least 80% contact and investigate old tickets. Days 31–60: resolve priority complaints and test fixes. Days 61–90: create growth plans for recovered merchants and monitor failure and usage.

Measurement

The proposed KPIs are contact rate, root-cause coverage, case resolution, reactivation, 30-day retention, failure rate and volume recovered. The source proposes an initial planning goal of reactivating 25% of the 312-merchant cohort (78 merchants) within 30 days; it is explicitly described as a planning target, not a forecast or achieved result.

Growth follows service recovery

The sequence is deliberate: restore reliability, rebuild usage, then grow responsibly. For Ifeoma Superstores, the source proposes recovering at least 80% of the ₦48m baseline, or ₦38.4m, after service issues are addressed. Pricing incentives are positioned as an approved commercial option—not the first response when the evidence points to service problems.

What this demonstrates

Merchant retention, churn-risk prioritisation, root-cause diagnosis, service recovery, cross-functional escalation, reactivation measurement, account planning and responsible expansion.

Project note: This is a strategy and operating-plan case study based on the supplied presentation. The recovery percentages and revenue figures above are case evidence or proposed targets from the source, not results achieved by the portfolio owner.

Case study 01 · National Malaria Chemoprevention Campaign

Helping users feel at home with the software.

Customer onboarding, user training and technical support for a digital campaign platform.

The challenge

More than 100 account users needed support to start using campaign software and digital data-collection tools. Users needed help understanding platform features, workflows and common usage challenges.

My approach

I supported users from onboarding and training through ongoing platform assistance. I guided users through the software, ODK and KoboCollect workflows, and handled questions through phone, live chat and email. I troubleshot account, data and platform issues, prioritised timely first responses and worked within established SLAs.

Follow-through

I documented tickets and resolutions in Zendesk, escalated unresolved technical issues and followed them through to closure. This helped maintain continuity and a consistent support experience.

What this demonstrates

Customer onboarding, SaaS user education, technical troubleshooting, ticket management, escalation ownership and continued customer support.

Impact

Case study 03 · Exagon Pharmaceutical Ltd

Turning a quiet account back into a conversation.

Proactive customer follow-up and relationship management to recover at-risk accounts.

The challenge

Some customer accounts had become inactive or showed signs that they were likely to churn. These relationships needed attention before disengagement became permanent.

My approach

I monitored and followed up with inactive and at-risk accounts, using targeted engagement and relationship management to reconnect with customers. I responded to enquiries and complaints, resolved service concerns where possible and escalated issues when necessary.

Customer-first follow-through

I focused on understanding concerns, keeping communication professional and following up to support timely outcomes. Account activity and next steps were maintained in HubSpot CRM.

What this demonstrates

Churn-risk awareness, proactive outreach, relationship management, complaint handling, customer retention and CRM hygiene.

Impact
92%

of accounts identified as likely to churn were recovered through targeted engagement.
